⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs.
  • Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that.
  • It has been revealed that this is where we are right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

It has been revealed that this is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

Industry observers note that GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

It has been revealed that we want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

It has been revealed that we suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

Recent findings suggest that no extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

Sources indicate that that is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

Recent findings suggest that the model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

Industry observers note that for models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Industry observers note that our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

Sources indicate that the llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

It has been revealed that transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

It has been revealed that when GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

Sources indicate that llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

Industry observers note that transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for fresh architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Sources indicate that our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

It has been revealed that faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

In a recent development, these changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

It has been revealed that the initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an problem with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘I gave up at least $6,000 and I’d do it again’.

Welcome to Friday and therefore to another edition of On Call, The Register's reader-contributed tech support column in which we share your tales of cleaning up messes made by clients and colleagues.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Dennis" who told us he once ran a tech support business in a major US city.

Recent findings suggest that "I got a call from a very well-known lawyer's office," he told On Call. "Over the two decades I spent supporting his office, this attorney and I became close friends.".

The attorney was also a good client because Dennis found himself billing a three-figure sum every month for malware removal that resulted from the lawyer’s – ahem – personal browsing habits.

Dennis eventually tired of malware removal and told his client to expect a substantial bill for the iMac he was about to buy as a replacement for his PC.

"I told him this would pay for itself in 18 months," Dennis wrote, because he figured it wouldn't get malware all the time.

"He actually said, with genuine concern: 'If you do that, you will make less money'.".

Dennis replied that he aimed to give his clients the best advice, and that on this occasion his counsel was to pay Apple instead of himself!

Sources indicate that "It took him about five years to stumble across anything that could harm that iMac," Dennis wrote. "When he did, I had no idea what to do: I had never seen an infected Apple product.".

So he did what all tech support people do: reinstalled the OS and crossed his fingers.

Dennis was rewarded when the machine came back to life, with all data and settings intact.

Industry observers note that "I had given up at least $6,000 in support revenue by solving his problem and I'd do it again," he wrote, before winding up his story by letting us know "I retired five years ago. It’s still on his desk!".

Have you done less tech support to deliver more value? If so, click here to send On Call an email and charge us with the responsibility of telling your story on a future Friday. ®.

  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • Sources indicate that AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

Sources indicate that AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

Sources indicate that as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly crucial sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

Sources indicate that this builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this latest phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Recent findings suggest that performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

In a recent development, the coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

According to recent reports, reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

It’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs.

It’s called DreamCoder, an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already.

I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold.

It has been revealed that one thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents.

Sources indicate that why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like.

Industry observers note that but a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal.

So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build.

And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be.

Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it.

Let’s roll back time to the 1950s.

Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history.

According to recent reports, john McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the Advice Taker, a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called commonsense reasoning using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI.

Industry observers note that in the 50s there was little in the way of computer software that could do this. To formalize such a system you need a lot of data, rigorously formatted, and a method of manipulating the data. The data and code itself may intertwine recursively, and so an ordinary programming language would not work.

It has been revealed that to help him achieve this, McCarthy created the LISt Processing (LISP) language made up of two facets: M-expressions, a functional language in the vein of Algol; and S-expressions, designed for symbolic data representation, and never intended as a method of writing code. S-expressions were dolled up with parentheses. M-expressions meanwhile used square brackets to visually separate the two. Uniquely, the language specification had an eval feature that would prove that the language is also a universal Turing machine… if only McCarthy had the means to do so. It was theoretical because McCarthy lacked, in time, staff and money, what he needed build this recursive evaluator that can take as input its own world state and evaluate it alongside new expressions, a fact made even more apparent by the sheer complexity of his M-expression language and the limited resources he had at the time.

Sources indicate that steve Russell who worked with him proved him wrong the way most young people do: by just doing it. Russell wrote the first LISP Interpreter with a working eval function, but M-expressions got sidelined; the imperative, procedural nature of programming got squished into S-expressions instead. They had to hand roll the language on paper then punch it into cards and then batch run them. Eliding M-expressions was a simple matter of pragmatism. And so LISP was born. And through several accidents of history, M-expressions never gained traction. M-expressions live on in Wolfram’s Mathematica, but few other places.

Much later, McCarthy eventually conceded that,.

“One can even conjecture that LISP owes its survival specifically to the fact that its programs are lists, which everyone, including me, has regarded as a disadvantage.”.

It has been revealed that S-expressions were always intended as the storage format with a bridge language to manipulate them. But by pushing evaluation into the same symbolic representation format as the data, we have what we call LISP today. That is why LISP is so unique. Consider a simple calculator. (+ 2 2) can simultaneously represent an expression that we want to compute, two plus two, or perhaps a ledger of record of a calculation we have already done.

Recent findings suggest that mcCarthy never built the Advice Taker in its purest form. He and his team ran into many philosophical, mathematical and computational walls that kept them occupied for a long time.

In a recent development, the idea behind the Advice Taker was simple. If you want to go somewhere in your car, you can symbolically express this by building a chain of narrative facts – kinda like a flowchart, but as small snippets of rules and facts, not as one grand design.

The system would automatically resolve ambiguities, and all the logician had to do was capture the microcosm of the world he wished to represent:.

According to recent reports, and so on. If you’re a student of Computer Science you’ll see echoes of Prolog here. The intent was simple: if we can symbolically express the world around us, we can advise that symbolic world with real-life facts, and have the automaton that uses this reified symbolic world change with it.

But the axiomatic complexity of a world model would never survive an encounter with a 3-year-old child. Every axiom you write begets a new one — so you can walk to your front door? Well what if the door is locked? Or what if your car is parked on the street and not in your drive way?

Industry observers note that A rules-based order of the world is a tender, beautiful one; but it is hard to build. It’s a fractal of ever-more specific and pedantic rules that conspire against you, just as you think you have a soluble world, typed and ready.

Anyone who has ever written Prolog knows exactly what that feels like!

I have my own personal story to add to this. In the 90s as a teenager I got a summer internship at a business that built banking software. They clearly didn’t know what to do with us teenaged interns, so on our first day they crammed us in a room and split us into teams and told us to build a flow chart for assembling a bike. Team exercise or something. Best one wins. We were told to be as specific and explicit as possible and account for as many conditions as we could think of, and the poor employees who had to mind us did their best to help. I distinctly recall losing because in my flowchart I forgot to open the box the disassembled bike came in.

McCarthy meanwhile eventually moved on and set up his own AI lab at Stanford, but the idea of the Advice Taker lived on.

In the late 70s Stallman and Steele create EMACS (Editing MACroS), also at MIT’s AI Lab, a set of building blocks on top of TECO, a famously inscrutable text editor. TECO did not upgrade the screen by default; you had to toggle that on and hope your edits worked. You typed out terse keyboard commands, crossed your fingers and hoped you got it right, and then you patiently waited for your text manipulation to take effect. Rinse and repeat until you got what you wanted.

In a recent development, stallman and Steele wanted more: they wanted macros so they could automate tedium of typing all that line noise. This strand of augmentation and later on self-modification is of course a unifying theme in Emacs today. The history of Emacs is long; but its outcome is known to us. I am typing this very article in Richard Stallman’s Emacs.

McCarthy’s Advice Taker left its mark in a subtle but indelible way. Warren Teitelman built the ADVISE system in his thesis with a cool title that reads like something out of a pulpy 1970s sci-fi novella: PILOT: A Step Toward Man-Computer Symbiosis. Teitelman, he later stated, was deeply inspired by McCarthy’s original idea of advising systems.

Recent findings suggest that in his thesis, he describes a method of arresting a function call and inserting code before or after it is run. He was tired of editing other people’s LISP code by hand, and wanted a way of modifying their code without touching it directly. He built and rebuilt his system several times over the years, culminating in his ADVISE system in Interlisp, a structured editor and language runtime for manipulating LISP code and data. Interlisp eschewed plain text files; instead, you manipulated the tree at a high level of abstraction with explicit instructions like “move X list to Y position”. You can see my own attempts at merging structured editing with plaintext editing in Combobulate.

According to recent reports, MIT AI hackers eventually implemented Teitelman’s ADVISE system from his PILOT thesis in their own versions of Emacs. Later, it was canonized in Chalupsky’s own 1992 re-implementation in Emacs Lisp that lives on (M-x find-library advice.el) as one of Emacs’s advice systems to this day.

What began as an idea for expressing automata using symbolism in an as-yet theoretical language in the 1950s culminated in a system for dynamically altering functions in GNU Emacs in the 1990s. What an unlikely lineage and history.

Symbolism and AI did not end with advising functions. There were many attempts at symbolic intelligence. Terry Winograd’s SHRDLU; Marvin Minsky’s Frame Systems; and even Emacs’s ELIZA-style M-x doctor all make use of symbolic “AI”.

None of them brought us closer to the AI that proponents of symbolic AI hoped they would.

In hindsight that seems obvious.

Writing a LISP macro just so will not produce artificial intelligence; nor will a carefully crafted web of rules and symbolic algebra suddenly spark intelligence. We know that today, but for a generation of computer scientists it felt like the future we have all read about in science fiction novels: a perfect, logical intelligence. A positronic brain. Robby the Robot; HAL 9000; C-3PO; Data; or the Speedies and Cuties from I, Robot. The unifying theme of these science fiction stories is they are automatons that follow strict rules — they obey Asimov’s three Laws of Robotics.

Every turn of hardware and software brought them ever closer to one day realizing the vision of an artificial intelligence, captured in neat axioms and LISP S-expressions, and modified in tools like Emacs.

It is surprising that symbolic AI, the vanguard movement for artificial intelligence, would instead dissipate into the wider body of Computer Science and programming as tools, languages and concepts, but not survive as a viable method of achieving AI.

Perhaps we always knew. Because at some point – even if we never really fully internalized it – we discovered that a ductile system that is shaped by its master’s desires is a tool that survives the ages because it remains eternally useful.

A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence.

For all the mathematical purity, beauty even, of the idea of a clockwork mind that is introspectable and malleable and its behavior expressed as S-expressions and interpreted by elegant algorithms and honed macros, we can, through the benefit of hindsight – now that we do have AI through other means – see that it was not to be.

In a recent development, the argument in favor of ductility is especially poignant when you learn of the Connectionists, which sounds like a bad 1960s band, but was in fact a loose coalition of people who believed firmly that neural networks, not symbolic AI, were the path to success. The Connectionist viewpoint was deeply unpopular in AI academia of that era, and funding for it was scarce.

Frank Rosenblatt invented the Perceptron, a foundational concept in neural networks, in 1957. Before Rosenblatt died in 1971, Marvin Minsky, an authority in the AI movement at MIT and a leading proponent of Symbolism, knifed the idea of Perceptrons and neural networks in a book he co-authored with Seymour Papert. They named the book, which they also dedicated to Rosenblatt, Perceptrons. The book deftly explains the mathematics of Perceptrons but undercuts their possible utility by showing that a single-layer Perceptron cannot represent an XOR gate. It was a deliberately obtuse reading of what neural networks could and could not do. With one additional hidden layer, a network can represent an XOR gate. It was a sneaky thrust of the stiletto: Minsky’s claims were overstated. A fact that was not lost on anybody in the Symbolic or Connectionist camps.

It’s disputed if the Perceptrons book led to the first AI winter in the 1970s. It certainly did not help. But funding for many AI research paths dried up in the 1970s.

The Connectionist movement was vindicated in the long run. They lost the battle then, but they won the war, and the fruits of their research eventually gave us AI.

Sources indicate that the ductility we so prize in our software and tools today is antithetical to a strict, symbolic world model spun of axioms and facts that we hoped would one day birth AI. Yet to try and give birth to this world they had to build the most ductile tools of them all: LISP and, from that, also software like Emacs. The ultimate hacker’s tool.

It is ironic then that a neural network, a crude facsimile of how a brain works, a construct that is by its nature ductile and malleable, won out in the end.

So I feel a profound sadness that I started out programming DreamCoder in Emacs, the most extensible editor in the world, by hand back in May 2025, only to see DreamCoder write itself… in DreamCoder today.

In a recent development, I am still sad, but I also know that our industry completely reinvents itself every decade or two. This is my second career upheaval. Most programmers today have not been around long enough to go through it themselves. So I feel for them that this especially massive quake is their first encounter with how unsentimental our industry is.

But for all the sadness, I wake up every day with a feeling of optimism that I have not felt in a very long time.

It has been revealed that I finally get to build again, no longer weighed down by my decades of knowledge and experience that held my ambition in check. I truly have not felt this liberated since I was a teenager programming in Delphi, blissfully unaware that the things I was busy building were impossible for a self-taught teenager to ever realize. I see this reflection in others: the best programmers I know also love AI. Amateurs also revel in AI’s capabilities, happy that they can finally solve problems they could never afford to pay a programmer to do for them.

I must admit that building software has, over the years, gotten a lot more complex, with an ever-larger share of that work being repetitive tedium. This is more so with hobby software – as I do not get paid to do it, so I do not have a moral duty to see it through – where I’d do all the fun bits leaving just the enervating, boring and soul-crushing parts behind. Do you have a projects folder full of sad, abandoned projects like I do?

According to recent reports, now I can craft in abundance. AI has freed up a lot of toil but I somehow still find myself busy all day doing real work.

Sources indicate that building a coding harness is perhaps the closest I will get to the optimism all those researchers and scientists must have felt in the 1970s and 1980s. They hoped that with a little bit more work, their logical rules would kindle a newly introduced intelligence. Fifty years on, and I can simply tell DreamCoder to improve itself and watch as it changes before me. I can ask the AI running inside it to analyze the changes I have made to its tools and prompt and have it adjust them accordingly. It feels like science fiction; the very thing the researchers of yesterday strove to build. Yet we really do live in this reality now.

Sources indicate that so. DreamCoder. Let me address the 900 lb gnu in the room: DreamCoder is not an Emacs-related application. The reason is unfortunately one of economics and access: I want to build an AI coding harness for everyone. But don’t worry: I have some cool intends for DreamCoder + Emacs, and AI + Emacs more generally going forward. So stay tuned.

In a recent development, but what about all those other coding harnesses? Well, most of those harnesses all suffer from the same mistakes. It is a problem that is not unique to coding harnesses or the people who make them, but a constraint we all labor under, and one that is not easily replaced by AI:.

Taste is a scarce, human resource.

Sources indicate that and for all the bounty of AI, it still requires a human to persevere and to see things through. One thing intensive use of AI coding has taught me is that we’re going to need a lot of computer programmers who know what they’re doing going forward. I believe this is so, because let us be honest, most people do not want to program computers, even if that computer can actually do the bulk of the work for them. It requires a steady hand to build reliable software; that has not changed.

Therefore, if we programmers have to spend a lot of our time interacting with AI, then the tool we do it with should be ‘human-centric’ in its design, and it should take advantage of all the modern features we have at our disposal.

Back in May 2025 I took a look at all the tooling and remarked “no, thank you.” Today I look at the landscape and I feel pretty much the same.

And I think I am not the only one who feels that way. Most of these coding harnesses, to me, feel bristly. They shouldn’t be; but they are like that because we are at an important inflection point where no one really knows what the future looks like. We’re all just… fumbling around a bit. It’s an exciting time to build software, even if we don’t quite know what the world will look like a few years hence.

One thing I am adamant about is that DreamCoder must be a powerful, frontier-class coding harness. That means it should have all the features you’d expect from that: backgroundable sub agents, MCP servers, cache efficiency, and all that stuff. Check.

Industry observers note that but that stuff quickly recedes into the background because, you know, it just works. Day to day you will dart between chats and terminals and whatnot, and you need an interface that accommodates that. Emacs is a tiling window manager; so is DreamCoder. DreamCoder’s window manager is a little bit cleverer than most window managers as every pane has a minimum, comfortable and maximum size. The window manager will therefore ensure windows always fit snugly on your screen, and you’ll never end up in a situation where windows are tiny and unreadable. It has a sophisticated constraint satisfaction solver that tries to balance your demand for a fresh window (“open a terminal”) with the challenge of keeping your visible panes roughly the same size. If DreamCoder can’t wedge in a new pane, it’ll punt one to the hidden window bar. Just click it to resurface it, or hover it to see what it’s doing; it’s a live view.

Because of my Emacs roots, I think a good tool must be keyboard-friendly. Because it runs on a browser you get the mouse for free of course. But smacking the tab button over and over is a frustrating user experience in complex webapps, and doubly so a tiling window manager: where exactly are you going to end up when you tab from one window to the next? To combat that, I built an avy-style window and “point of interest” selector for chats. Tap a key and pick from a selection of “embark”-like actions such as clicking links or opening pictures. It’s a work in progress, but I think it works well.

Most high-volume operations like opening and creating panes is done through a Helm-like interface with search-as-you-type. It’s really efficient, of course. And it works with a mouse also; which is sort of the point. The keyboard’s there for those who want it, and the mouse for regular folk who are just getting started. One unique feature of the design, which admittedly I am still exploring privately, is that everything is stored as Javascript objects (on account of running in your browser) so it’s not too much of a leap to build “macros” that prefill most of these dialog windows, leaving behind just the fields you want to edit.

But yeah. With DreamCoder I want to take the best of Emacs and its coterie of third-party packages and bring some of that with me. The world is still not ready for an Emacs-shaped future, sadly, so that is why DreamCoder is a standalone application and a web frontend.

Another thing that drives me wild: I see people with tmux running 10 claude codes (or codex, or…) cycling between them like a duck gallery at a carnival to see if one of them is done working, or if it needs human intervention.

In a recent development, so there’s two things to unpack here: one is running lots of things in parallel, and the other is observability. You need insight into what is going on: is an AI jammed because it’s awaiting an answer or a tool safety prompt? Perhaps you’ve parked a bunch of chats pending some conversations with coworkers or other work that must finish first.

In DreamCoder you have workspaces. They’re like virtual desktops (or window configurations in Emacs lingo): a snapshot view of panes as you want em. As you can see from the screenshots, panes expand to fill all the space. So if you want more space, you can: resize them (with the mouse or keyboard); shuffle them to a named workspace; or float them so they sit on top of the other windows.

But if you’ve got a lot of things happening in multiple workspaces, it’s hard to keep tabs on that. That’s why DreamCoder has a massive, honking minimap in the top-right corner. One for each workspace. The minimap is a miniature of your actual layout. Each pane in the map gently pulses when it’s working, and it makes it abundantly clear when it’s blocked. When there’s nothing to do, it’s green.

Because workspaces and panes are distinct things you interact with, it must be easy to navigate between them.

I also wanted full-on, optional Emacs key bindings, but that is… pretty much impossible to properly build. Browsers lock you out of some rather important Emacs button combinations. Sadly that feature is parked until I can solve it on all major browsers without breaking your normal browser keys.

According to recent reports, that’s not to say it doesn’t have Emacs-inspired key bindings. Most global actions are reachable with Alt+x, akin to M-x; local, pane-specific ones with Alt+c. Alt+m activates keyboard mode: you can now type the number of the named pane to jump to it; or WASD to switch the active pane in that cardinal direction.

Support for open weight models like Qwen, Gemma, Deepseek, GLM, etc. is also very important to me. They work so well. I’m really surprised, here in late 2026, just how capable small models are at local-only development compared to just one year ago. Qwen 3.8 27B, for example, is fantastically good for its size. You can do a lot of good software development with it if you’re a capable hand yourself. Bigger models equal more auto piloting; but that Qwen model? Wow. So local models work great. In fact I think the future is local for a lot of use cases. Intelligence is fast approaching a cost where it will be too cheap to meter. If you remember the personal computer revolution in the 1980s and 1990s, then there are definitely echoes of that here.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve been holding off on local models then I do recommend you reconsider. Small ones like Qwen 3.8 27B (or its cousin, Flash Next) can run well on a high-end gaming rig or Mac, or with a little investment if you do not have that. If you have a dinky old computer and you’re cash starved, then not all hope is lost. Turn to the potato agronomists on twitter: give twitter’s AI, Grok, what you have and what you can reasonably spend and tell it to track down the cutting edge setup for your rig. This is no lie the fastest, easiest way to catch up to the cutting edge of self-hosted inference today. Five minutes.

According to recent reports, as I’ve been building DreamCoder, I have come to the belief I’m not just building a coding harness. Coding harnesses are an IDE for the future; it will do more than just display a chat window for coding agent work. DreamCoder does more than that already. It’s going the way of Emacs in that it’ll consume a wide range of adjacent workflows and tools. But I have only just gotten started. I am brimming with ideas I’m building in parallel, but they take time because as I remarked it’s not about the code; it’s just one small facet of building something that works well. But you know that already: it’s always the last mile.

DreamCoder is the most ambitious, technically complex and advanced software project I have ever built in my life. And that’s just the beginning. I’m not done. I’ve barely started. I will be blogging about this going forward, in addition to my usual Emacs scribblings.

In fact, the thing I’m right now grinding away at is a world-class pentest and cybersecurity suite in DreamCoder. Every single bit of software we have ever written is vulnerable; we have many rough years ahead of us. Just look at the crippling vulnerabilities coming out every day now almost. Even the most security conscious person is going to find themselves on the wrong side for no other reason than we depend on packages that were mature and stable and assumed to be secure. DreamCoder can do its bit to help catch many of most obvious weaknesses, especially as newly introduced software is minted every day that also needs thorough testing.

To round it off, I would like to formally invite you to join me in making DreamCoder better by trying it out. It’s great. It’s not a toy; it’s not a demo; and it’s not a weekend prototype. It’s a frontier coding harness that has most of what you’d expect: MCP, backgroundable sub agents and shell commands, terminal windows, skills, hooks, 99% cache hit, it runs for days, and an interactive UI for all of it. There’s a handy dandy importer for your Pi, OpenCode or Codex configs also to help you get started. A couple of clicks and your model settings are set up in DreamCoder. Ready to go.

Ubuntu Core Desktop targets 28.04 debut, with default status in its sights

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canonical's stretch goal is to make the immutable OS standard in 30.04 – without retiring the traditional distro.
  • Canonical is targeting Ubuntu 28.04 LTS for the release of its immutable Core Desktop, with a stretch goal of making it the default download for Ubuntu 30.04.
  • Canonical's VP of engineering, Jon Seager, set out the timetable in his opening keynote at Ubuntu Summit 26.10.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canonical's stretch goal is to make the immutable OS standard in 30.04 – without retiring the traditional distro.

Canonical is targeting Ubuntu 28.04 LTS for the release of its immutable Core Desktop, with a stretch goal of making it the default download for Ubuntu 30.04.

Canonical's VP of engineering, Jon Seager, set out the timetable in his opening keynote at Ubuntu Summit 26.10. Yes, we know, we have heard this before: we reported on his prepares last month. But this time, there's the beginning of a release schedule.

Seager mentioned that Ubuntu Core is already out there in tens of thousands of IoT devices – which seems like a modest estimate to us, and to him too, as he quickly added "maybe more." Despite some noise a few years ago, though, what's still missing is the desktop version.

Seager's slides listed three bullet points: that Core Desktop will be "immutable," "composable," and "attestable.".

As he put it, they are "taking the whole of the Linux operating system, and cramming the whole thing into snaps." Acknowledging that this is going to be wildly controversial, he said: "This is one for the Redditors.".

Recent findings suggest that he's right. There is a lot of resistance to snap, and in direct response, advocacy of the Red Hat-backed Flatpak instead – but we have seen almost none that is based on either system's technical merits. Much of that opposition concerns claims of one being more open than the other. We've looked at how both systems work, and our impression is that the implementation of snap is cleaner, simpler, easier to use, and more comprehensible. Snap does depend on systemd, which Flatpak does not – but only for now. Flatpak NG is in development and will also need everyone's favorite init system.

Industry observers note that ubuntu Core's immutability is not newly introduced technology: even Core 16 is now a decade old. It has supported in-place version upgrades since Core 22.

According to recent reports, we have reported before that Canonical remains strongly committed to its packaging format, and that commitment seems stronger than ever. Seager continued: "Never has a model like snap confinement been more relevant… we're finally in a position where we can bring this to the desktop.".

The core idea of an immutable OS is that "much more of the system is not writable at runtime," meaning that it "can't be messed with once the system has booted." He talked about the same three use cases we discussed last month. The "browser-centric machine" is the company's analog to Google ChromeOS, and he remarked that it's essentially ready now, suggesting that everyone listening probably has a family member whose computer is basically just a way to use a web browser.

In a recent development, the second was the dedicated games machine, which we interpret as a response to Valve's SteamOS. This edition, he remarked, would "boot straight to Steam," with "just enough of a shell to launch games." There's also an immutable "development workstation," and here, he offered the example of developers who need to work on some long-unsupported hardware or software, for whom an immutable OS means that you "can't brick your system by installing some weird old dependencies, unmaintained for 20 years.".

Sources indicate that another notable benefit is "atomic, transactional updates," which he noted "brings enormous stability." The terminology comes from the database world: an atomic operation succeeds as a whole or is not applied. The aim is to avoid leaving the system stranded between incompatible package versions, with rollback providing a route back if an patch causes trouble.

Ubuntu VP of Engineering Jon Seager.

The "composable" part means assembling the OS from separately packaged components, from desktop environments to underlying services such as PipeWire and fingerprint-reader support.

It has been revealed that here, Seager used an example that spoke to us. He asked: "Ever installed something and watch as it spewed stuff all over your system?" Yes, we have, many, many times. You install one innocent-seeming little component, and it brings in a database, three upcoming server components, and about half of a different desktop environment. We mentioned an example when we described how to customize Xfce a couple of months ago. That time around, in Debian, we found it was safe to install all packages starting with "xfce4-" except "xfce4-dev-tools." Most are tiny panel controls taking just hundreds of kilobytes, but the "dev-tools" package also pulls in several hundred megabytes of compilers, linkers, and other programming tools, totally unrelated to desktop layouts – and once installed, they're surprisingly tricky to remove again.

Industry observers note that this is part of the appeal of a composable immutable OS: adding a component need not mean tangling its dependencies into the base system. But easier housekeeping isn't the only attraction. Canonical kept snap packages from its cancelled phone and tablet OS because snaps enable it to maintain a single package of, for instance, Firefox, which will work on all of its different OS versions that are still getting updates. Moving such important external dependencies into isolated snap packages makes it easier and safer to upgrade from one version of the OS to another. Complex sets of dependencies are the main point of failure of OS upgrades, especially when the OS has been used for a while.

This is very much not a solved problem. For instance, Debian version upgrades can be fraught – especially when the installation has decades of history behind it. Debian does at least support version-to-version upgrades. For many years and versions, RHEL did not – which is why we highlighted AlmaLinux's tooling for the task. Zorin OS added version-to-version upgrades in 16.3 just a few years ago. Linux Mint introduced its own upgrade tooling a few years earlier, although it still imposes restrictions.

It has been revealed that it's a tough matter to crack. Major enterprise vendors discourage it, and phone OSes are all immutable. Helping with this problem is one of the main reasons snap packaging exists, while Flatpak is almost entirely irrelevant to it.

Sources indicate that seager also stated that Core Desktop would support "multiple desktops from the start." This will not be a GNOME-only project. Indeed, he specifically mentioned a KDE Plasma version, saying: "Plasma is great. People love it. We will have a KDE edition, with rolling Plasma. We will deliver upstream Plasma, as fast as we can." That sounds like a very welcome counterpoint to the LTS version of Plasma 6.6 in Kubuntu 26.04 whose announcement we covered back in August.

It has been revealed that for the "attestable" line of the slide, he claimed that Core Desktop was "evolving the way we think about 'trust' on a machine. We have TPM, secure boot, TPM-backed Full Disk Encryption… but they're all bolt-ons." Core Desktop, he added, could "tie this into a hardware root of trust," delivering "verified system integrity." Canonical revived its TPM-backed full-disk encryption system back in 2025, and it arrived in Ubuntu 26.04. Back in January, systemd creator Lennart Poettering introduced his startup Amutable, and earlier this month published a technical overview of its latest immutable Linux. We suspect Canonical is watching closely, and that this is a hint in that direction.

We were also amused by Seager's mention of another rather niche distro: he remarked that Core Desktop would deliver "all of the joy that people derive from NixOS, for those with that perverse habit – but for everybody.".

Daily preview installation images of Core Desktop will, apparently, be available very soon, in both GNOME and KDE flavors, and he warned that "there be dragons." (That may be a veiled nod to one of founder Mark Shuttleworth's other companies.).

After the promises made in 2023, we'll be watching that timetable closely. "I believe this is the future of Linux," Seager said, promising "a final version by 28.04, released alongside Ubuntu," adding that a "very stretchy stretch goal was by default for 30.04: download from ubuntu.com and you get Core Desktop – unless you ask for the other thing.".

According to recent reports, for those alarmed by that prospect, he had reassurance: "Ubuntu as you know it today is not going anywhere. There are no plans for the existing distro to go away.".

According to recent reports, core Desktop wasn't even the main subject of his keynote. They followed a lengthy excursion into formal logic: definitions, proofs, invariants, and designing software whose behavior can be checked against precisely stated rules. The accompanying slides showed the logos of organizations working in this area, such as Hegel, Antithesis, and the Lean programming language. For now, an entire OS is much too massive to formally verify, but subcomponents may be doable – and Canonical is starting with snapd.

He also expressed his satisfaction with the Stonking release, highlighting that it advanced Canonical's move toward Rust-based components, including Rustls and upki – noting that this proved very timely in the light of recent events. The release also delivered the newest available kernel, OpenSSL 4 – which he called a "huge change" – and official RISC-V images. He also called out the Myna speech-recognition feature, saying that it was all in-house, designed and shipped in six months by a team of "about two and a half people." It will form part of the company's prepares for what it calls a context-aware desktop. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • Sources indicate that an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

Sources indicate that an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

In a recent development, an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Recent findings suggest that every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

Sources indicate that the frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

Industry observers note that the RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Industry observers note that framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

Recent findings suggest that the viewer indicates the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

Sources indicate that the Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Recent findings suggest that here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

Recent findings suggest that the command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

Industry observers note that neMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

Recent findings suggest that the best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

According to recent reports, we opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

Industry observers note that the bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

Recent findings suggest that if you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Optional patch fixes misleading Android error for versions 25H2 and 26H2.
  • Sources indicate that A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded.
  • Industry observers note that the problem occurs when customers sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Optional patch fixes misleading Android error for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

Sources indicate that A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

Industry observers note that the problem occurs when customers sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again.".

Recent findings suggest that except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored.".

Recent findings suggest that cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft states the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID.

Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected.

An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets.

Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, consumers can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, holo4 is our new series of agentic models.
  • According to recent reports, holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • Recent findings suggest that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

According to recent reports, holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Recent findings suggest that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

Industry observers note that automationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

In a recent development, trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276.
