#92844. Tech Report: Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3311 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • According to recent reports, beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Industry observers note that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the newly introduced US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

According to recent reports, beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Industry observers note that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post highlights you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

Industry observers note that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

In a recent development, the two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

In a recent development, attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

Industry observers note that the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

It has been revealed that only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

According to recent reports, beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

It has been revealed that pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

According to recent reports, beam's config defines an expert-parallel strategy. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

Sources indicate that for faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Recent findings suggest that both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Sources indicate that below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

In a recent development, don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

It has been revealed that the quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

Sources indicate that after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

According to recent reports, training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Recent findings suggest that reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can patch the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the latest weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

According to recent reports, revision: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Sources indicate that optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

In a recent development, evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

Industry observers note that the next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one revision behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Industry observers note that you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

According to recent reports, at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

Industry observers note that for the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

It has been revealed that our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

Industry observers note that we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

In a recent development, first, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Sources indicate that beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

That’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Recent findings suggest that thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

In a recent development, this is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

Recent findings suggest that one question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

Zellij is a relatively latest entrant in the terminal-multiplexer category. Like GNU Screen and tmux it gives consumers the ability to manage a workspace inside a terminal with split panes, provides session management, and so forth; but Zellij also includes a web server for browser access to a terminal session, is extensible via a plugin API, and is likely more beginner-friendly than its predecessors. Its most recent release, version 0.46, adds a standalone terminal emulator, a built-in inbox for notifications, and a settings screen so users can configure the application without fussing with configuration files. While the low version number might suggest that it is not yet ready for serious use, it seems stable and full-featured enough to meet the needs of many users.

Redict deprecated in favor of Valkey

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Drew DeVault has revealed that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated.
  • I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose.
  • We recommend that Redict users switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects.

Drew DeVault has revealed that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated. He recommends switching to Valkey, the permissively licensed Redis fork supported by the Linux Foundation. The two projects are mutually compatible, so switching should be as simple as changing which package is installed and renaming the configuration file.

I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose. However, with the valkey project's success, and Redis's return to a copyleft license, Redict was not able to build a sustainable community.

We recommend that Redict users switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects. We advise against switching back to Redis; though it is once again open source, and copyleft, it uses a contributor license agreement which will facilitate another rug-pull when Redis has a bad financial quarter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TorchNeuron provides a upcoming native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • It has been revealed that torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a fresh backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TorchNeuron provides a upcoming native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

It has been revealed that torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a fresh backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

Recent findings suggest that to date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

Recent findings suggest that torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

Recent findings suggest that for the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

It has been revealed that the following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

According to recent reports, parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

It has been revealed that nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

Sources indicate that the command below introduces training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

According to recent reports, training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Recent findings suggest that make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, owners can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

#92840. Tech Report: AWS got hit by an outage too. Here's why you didn't hear about it

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (848 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: AWS got hit by an outage too. Here's why you didn't hear about it

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If a service falls in the forest and nobody hears it...
  • My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?".
  • In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn got salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If a service falls in the forest and nobody hears it...

My editor asked me this week "why is everything except AWS breaking?".

It's a great question! They haven't been in the headlines! In fact, as they are wont to do, AWS spokesperson Patrick Neighorn got salty to a reporter about how unreliable Downdetector is when it started showing them as impacted.

According to recent reports, if you'll permit me a small digression, this stems from a misunderstanding of what Downdetector is for. Historically the AWS status site was so hilariously slow to reflect the lived customer experience that some jackass (me) built a rewriter that sits at stop.lying.cloud to make it a smidgen more realistic. As a result, the question people are really trying to answer when they visit Downdetector is "my app just broke; is it my crappy code or is there a global event going on?" There are mitigations for both, but they look nothing alike.

In a recent development, AWS view crowdsourced reports of the form "the internet is broken, must be AWS" as a stain upon their honor. In fact, it's a badge of their own success, as "the internet" and "AWS" have become inextricably linked in people's minds.

But back to my editor's question, "why didn't AWS go down?".

AWS now has 34 generally available commercial regions, of which two are presently smoking craters due to the Iran conflict. Each of these has hundreds of services that AWS offers to customers, of which a dozen or so are high quality, if I'm being characteristically uncharitable. They experience degradation in various ways, and they go largely unnoticed.

But on November 15, AWS confirmed an incident that disrupted 11 of those ~12 good services in their oldest and most crucial region, us-east-1.

In a recent development, at 3:05 AM PST, they stated that they started seeing sign-up errors, authentication concerns, and connectivity issues. Five minutes later engineers were engaged. Not to be outdone, their status page swung into action after a leisurely coffee, and posted its first indication of an incident 93 minutes later. (See previous comments on stop.lying.cloud). The all-clear demonstrated up at 6:53 AM.

In a recent development, every site has downtime. Sometimes it blows up publicly, other times nobody seems to notice. Heck, AWS mentioned in September that it had experienced permanent data loss in its two smoking craters, but after that news cycle passed I haven't heard a thing about it. I do think it's patently unreasonable to blame them for this specific problem; "acts of war" are kinda hard to predict from the corporate planning meeting.

According to recent reports, A few things combined to help AWS out on November 15. First, it was pre-dawn Pacific time on Sunday. Most of us slept through it; my kids aren't even up that early.

Further, the services that were most impacted (IAM Identity Center) were for engineers signing in to AWS accounts, not consumers staring at an app that stopped working.

Plus, the competition sucked all the oxygen out of the room: a day-plus Microsoft 365 364 outage and a four-hour nationwide air traffic ground stop had done a great job of level-setting what kind of outage was going to get attention, and "us-east-1 being weird but the apps still work" doesn't cut it.

Downdetector – which is owned by Accenture, so it's not like AWS doesn't have a throat to choke if they want to stop picking on reporters – measures consumer screaming. Originally, it was largely Twitter semantic analytics. This isn't a bad thing! As I said, I want to know if the internet is breaking. We can sort out exactly what part later.

The November 15 outage didn't produce that kind of screaming. Ironically, the tool that AWS is complaining about in the newspaper is the reason they skated by without notice on this outage.

Counterintuitively, Downdetector reports that outages have decreased since about 2022. Instead, what we're seeing is large-scale centralization.

Sources indicate that our companies don't run email systems internally anymore; we outsource to large technology companies who are almost universally better at fixing and resolving large-scale issues than we will be internally. And it feels unkind to dunk on those hard-working folks for their outages; would we want them to dunk on us for ours?

("Wait, don't you own stop.lying.cloud?" "Do as I say, not as I do.").

But whether anyone notices depends upon what layer broke, and when. If my organization's email system broke on Monday, and your company's email system broke on Tuesday, the story would stop at "computers suck." But when everyone's email system goes down at once, the world takes notice.

Microsoft had to tell the whole world about a bug it mostly sat on since July. AWS hasn't had to tell anyone anything. My editor runs a tech publication that covers this stuff for a living and didn't know. You can't buy PR like this, and AWS didn't have to.

If I were AWS, I'd stop complaining about Downdetector and send it a fruit basket. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Modernising Retail at Scale: Architecting a Cloud‑to‑Edge Platform for a Global Enterprise.

Industry observers note that jayesh Bhayani discusses Tesco’s decade-long enterprise transformation from fragmented legacy systems to a unified cloud-edge platform. He explains how aligning system, talent, and process modernizations allowed Tesco to scale mission-critical retail operations to millions of customers, while sharing practical lessons on build vs. buy, cloud cost management, and preparing for agentic commerce.

Jayesh Bhayani is Senior Engineering Director at Tesco, playing a central role in leading technology strategy and shaping business direction. His work focuses on creating strategic clarity, architectural direction, and organizational alignment needed for the business to compete at pace in an increasingly disruptive retail environment, driving enterprise scale and agentic commerce readiness.

Recent findings suggest that software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

It has been revealed that jayesh Bhayani: I'm going to spend some time in sharing our learnings of transformation at scale at Tesco. That's why modernizing technology at Tesco. How it has changed the culture, not just within the company, along with systems, but enabled the growth for the company. From that perspective, after 10 years being at Tesco, I thought it would be good to share the learnings we had from here and how we are looking at the future.

I was in California, in Silicon Valley, for about 25 years, when Tesco reached out to me, saying, would you like to work at Tesco? I had got no concept of Tesco, because I had never come to London before that. When I looked at the website, it was a pretty basic website. The outside-in perspective, when you look at the website of a large grocery chain, feels like there is no technology. This went on for a few months. After that, they convinced me to talk to a few people in the technology department. The state that this technology was, and what was needed for growth and the transformation that was needed at scale, was what motivated me and my wife. We were empty nesters already by that time. We decided, why not? Came here. Just around that time, Trump got elected. We felt even better.

First of all, some context into how large Tesco is. There are about 5,000 stores. Some of them are super. Some of them are medium. Some of them are small. They are across five different countries. We used to be in Asia as well, when I started 10 years back, in Thailand, Malaysia. We divested those businesses. We are still in five countries. We have 20 distribution centers. We have 25 million customers. That's almost one-third of the UK population. That's not small. We have 350,000 colleagues across our stores. Out of that, maybe around 15,000 in head office. Out of that, around 6,000 in technology. Again, it's big. It's big operations, large number of colleagues. We do around 50 million baskets. Not number of transactions, the baskets, which means the orders across our estate in our stores. We do 1.3 million online orders in a week. When COVID came, many companies talk about scale.

When COVID happened, when entire business shifted towards online, our challenge was to double the number of online slots that we can make available for our customers. By that time, for the e-commerce part, our platform was already live. When we doubled it, that's equivalent of putting almost three other competitor companies online in one month. Many companies stopped taking orders. Many companies stopped signing customers. We doubled it in a month. That again shows the scale. Fifty million cases through supply chain, huge. We are not even talking about number of miles the trucks travel and the logistics within the distribution center. We do 4.5 billion calls a day. We have 98% UK coverage when I talk about 25 million customers, but coverage-wise in terms of online business, that can cover the entire geography of UK. We cover almost 98%, which means you can have your home delivery of grocery done in 98% of the UK.

In a recent development, tills, as we call it here in the UK, POS systems, as called in many other countries, almost 50,000. That's just POS devices. We are not talking about all other thousands and tens of thousands of handheld devices that run on the same platform. That's just the context, because that sets a very different tone for the kind of technology, how mission-critical technology becomes. Then driving transformation through that is quite challenging, because I worked at startups. I've worked at mid-size companies. I had my own startup. Being in California and not having a startup is a crime. I tried that, too. I worked at Yahoo for 10 years. I worked at large companies, worked at startups. Tesco is yet another scale. I wanted to reflect here, because it drives quite a lot of complexities in decision-making of what would you do with your transformation and technology choices.

In a recent development, this goes beyond retail. Any industry that has got physical estate, digital, and real-time operations will face these complexities. That's where we learned about being both efficient and effective. Efficient is do things well, fast. Effective, do good things, which are more effective. A slight difference in nuances. You can be doing fast all the things, but if those are not the right things, you are chasing wrong goals. Do the right things and do things the right way, efficiency and effectiveness. I wanted to share here, this is not just about retail. This will apply to many of the industries who operate at that kind of scale and complexity.

Industry observers note that let's start as to why. Ten years back, why did we need transformation? It was quite a poor state within technology I'm talking. When they talked about a large grocery organization and I was thinking there is no technology inside, there was a lot of technology, but it was very siloed. Multiple technology stacks tied to historical business structures. When I'm talking siloed, this is not just, store had a POS system and e-commerce had something else. I'm talking multiple stacks within online or e-commerce business itself. Grocery, its entire stack. We had marketplace back then, completely different stack. One Microsoft, .NET, one Oracle. F&F, our clothing, Tesco wine. Customers across these, forget having single account, did not even have single login. Jayesh@groceryhomeshopping is different than Jayesh@marketplace, is different than Jayesh@f&f. We had no single customer view, no data platforms, no product management, nothing. It was that fragmented. There was no single identity, as I just explained.

Industry observers note that no single source of truth for stock or pricing. From that perspective, when you have multiple monolithic systems running in private data centers, we were not in public cloud back then. It was not even private data cloud. It was just a bunch of machines. You would be lucky if you asked for a server and you get a server in two months. That was the state. Decades old POS system, 20 years old software running on our POS systems in the stores, completely batch oriented. You couldn't connect to them. The deployments were the engineers would go with the floppy disk and then will deploy the software in the stores. Third-party solutions, not just third-party solutions, they were heavily customized, because when you are at the scale of Tesco, you can demand saying, I need a slightly different thing in your software. Sounds good initially. Then you're locked in with a very customized version of vendor solution for multiple years.

It has been revealed that we had software running from vendor solutions that were at least a decade old. You can't even upgrade them. Then heavily outsourced resources as well. These were where we had lots of consulting firms providing resources for us. Not a good culture, not good quality. You can imagine what the landscape was when we started 10 years back. At the scale of Tesco, that becomes quite complex to say, how do you find your journey through that?

It has been revealed that that got us the imperative for change, saying we definitely need omnichannel experience, because customer expectations were moving very fast. The old style of doing business was not working. Technology was not helping business. Business had all the motivation to change. Technology was stuck. We had hit the wall, literally. Global coherence across physical and digital estate, both. Rapid change cycles. Back then, as I noted, if you talked to a vendor and asked for a solution in our POS systems, it would be six months for minor changes. Regression on top of that, so three things would be broken. You do the testing, and they charge you for fixing the bugs again. It would be six to nine months before you could get anything out on our Tills or POS systems in stores. Forget e-commerce. Then along with that, of course, we needed higher reliability, higher capability. We needed omnichannel experience, higher security, everything.

In a recent development, it needed more capability and capacity, both. That led to us chasing from fragmented stacks to unified platforms that could serve all our channels across all our markets and develop a multi-tenant platform. That's what we developed. In a recent development, some business person would have a favorite person in technology, as I said, it was a phone call away. No one knew about technology. It has been revealed that tech excellence. Tech excellence is not just tech debt. We call it tech excellence, because it's proactive as well. It is not just, do we have a few bugs that we need to do? Or, do we need to patch our operating systems? Of course, yes. How are you taking care that you're not going to face into those challenges on an ongoing basis? Back then, there was no concept of total loss recovery. How do you blueprint for total loss recovery? This is not DR. DR is basic. When you're talking about total loss recovery, it's a completely different ballgame. The kinds of capabilities you need for that, we start to put that into tech excellence. Because it's very easily assumed, even within technology, and I'm not talking outside technology. Of course, business teams don't have that level of understanding. Outside technology, as well, at some point. Where now our business leaders talk about tech excellence saying, are you sure it's built right? It's needed. That's the cultural change we are talking about. That creates the framework for a much faster pace of delivery and clear ownership, as I said, with the clear domain boundaries, and strong and long-term resilience.

That strategic framework gave us, what are the core tenets of our platform? Only customer is not enough. Yes, we are driven by customer. That drives our business. Reuse across multiple different markets and business units.

Industry observers note that offline operations. When you are talking about thousands of edge devices working in your stores, one of the most critical requirements for us is a network can be flaky. Because if you get in the business of replacing network of your entire thing, you might be spending hundreds of millions. Grocery is a very low margin business, it's around 4%. Some are 3%, some are 4%, some are 4.5%. It's a very low margin business. Every penny that you spend counts, goes in your P&L. Cyber risk and compliance built-in into the platform. Super important. This is where we had to innovate across all three public clouds. We did create private cloud, not just a server sitting in our data centers, and edge platform as well. As I was just referring to low margin business, cost is a feature for us, not a constraint. We don't see cost as a constraint.

Industry observers note that it's a very different mindset. As part of one of our learnings, we'll go through the learnings, but since we are talking about that, when we jumped into public cloud, and this now will apply into agentic code development as well, and we are thinking through that. The value that gets created against the cost that you might be spending, you've got to be very careful about that. We were spending upwards of £50 million, £60 million on public cloud. I'm talking four, five years back. It was growing exponentially. If you don't control that, then you've got £50 billion business, which was back then, with 4% margin, you're talking about £2 billion. When you talk £100 million of just cloud cost, I'm not talking our salaries, I'm not talking about entire technology department, this is just cloud cost. You can imagine how much P&L you are impacting at that level. It's the responsibility of the technology department to say, how do you keep cost as a feature, not as a constraint?

Industry observers note that then we came up with good principles for our platform, which, as I stated, domain design was very important. Create composable services. Data pathways and data quality both matter. You need very clear data pathways as to how data would flow between the various different operating datasets to data lakes, but also data quality across each one of these steps. Security in a layered defense model, all the way from perimeter to built inside. We got tons of different layers of how do you think about security. Multi-tenancy by default, which is, you build the platform once. Even from the physical deployment perspective is the same deployment that works and enables multiple countries for us, multiple different businesses. Build product capabilities, not just solutions, not point solutions. Build products, build capabilities. Then abstractions, all of you will understand that. It's not just for hiding complexity but also when you got mobile applications running across thousands of microservices, running in the data center or in the cloud.

For example, add an item to your shopping cart has got at least 40 different microservices called. That's what went into our principles because that created cohesion across, as I was saying, digital and physical estate without becoming bottleneck.

Then, many of our large systems, we are talking about supply chain systems, distribution centers, technologies related to that, we tend to run that into our private cloud. Recent findings suggest that this is where as we are talking about agentic code development and everything, a developer could spend almost £500 a day without realizing or without clarity on what value is getting created. Sources indicate that what could have been better is, build central tech platform early. Portfolio management, we introduced that a bit late, but that where the products are matured when you're talking about 6,000 people in technology and hundreds of products, you need a very good management of where you are going to put your investment, where the value is. The portfolio management becomes very important. We use product maturity model for that now to say, our product is mature or not mature, and it can go left and right in the maturity curve.

Sources indicate that location strategy. Most companies, they assume that engineering can be even in-sourced where they are your own teams. They can be in various different locations, but if you're not careful, product management sits somewhere else, engineering sits somewhere else, program sits somewhere else. Try to create self-sufficient teams. I touched on three parts of those transformation, a little bit of each one of them to say what's key. There are many more in that one. The biggest point was the more you step back and think about it, you will avoid costly re-implementation and migration. That's huge. It spends a lot of time and spend of cost.

Final two slides on what are some of the tips if you are following the transformation at scale. Three pillars, we talked about that. Just system transformation is not enough. Change business processes when required, because they are just organically developed like your technology systems as well. Question that to say, is that really different? Why should four different countries have different operational processes? Simplify operation. Build core capabilities, we just talked about that. Because now we have the tech platform which supports this retail platform for those same CI/CDs, the observabilities, everything, but we could have started that early. Start that early. Throughput is a long game. Today also we get a lot of pressures, and can we go live in two months? Can we go live in two weeks? Can we go live in three weeks? We can do that if the platform capabilities are there. Total throughput is much higher today, but the same thing could have taken us six months long back when we had to develop those capabilities.

If we didn't do that, now we can do 10 such things and we would never have done that because we would have just duplicated it. Evolve continuously. We used to be very horizontally laid. I ran entire engineering of Tesco, all the platforms, all this thing, but product management was separate. Now that platforms are matured, we are going more vertical. I still run the platforms because that we cannot divide. The core platform is still there, but the application domain wise now we are creating more partnership between business and people like me within technology. Evolution is necessary. E-commerce is not just enough. Avoid tech for tech. Communicate value early. It's very hard to understand outside technology for sure. What are you all doing, is the frequent question we get. How come you are so many people? What's going on? It has gone less and less now. Even within technology, it's hard to explain what value we have created for the business.

We talked about the cost, IP and vendor lock-in. We are very careful when we are talking about agentic code development. We are very careful as to what kind of IP leakage could happen. Vendor lock-in, we talked about it. Even when we use many of the SaaS solutions, we ask for those protections from data sharing perspective, from IP perspective, so that we keep that edge of differentiation for Tesco. Then last one is technology will keep evolving, but if you have set the right culture, I mean there was blockchain there, public cloud before that, MapReduce systems, now agentic part. According to recent reports, if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

It has been revealed that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

According to recent reports, FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

Industry observers note that you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

In a recent development, every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the massive matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Industry observers note that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Industry observers note that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

Industry observers note that in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

The decoding kernel reveals up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

In a recent development, working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Sources indicate that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

Sources indicate that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

It has been revealed that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

It has been revealed that you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

In a recent development, work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Recent findings suggest that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

It has been revealed that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

Industry observers note that the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A major thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

Recent findings suggest that the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the fresh provider can't replay them.

In a recent development, API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

In a recent development, language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

Xint is reporting that it has discovered a collection of five critical vulnerabilities in the NGINX web server. The worst flaw, it says, would allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands on an affected nginx server with HTTP/2 enabled. The company also reports a local-privilege escalation (LPE) kernel vulnerability, which was introduced in the 4.15 kernel, in the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) subsystem. If chained with the NGINX vulnerability, it would allow an attacker to gain root privileges on the host. A kernel patch for this is not yet available.

Industry observers note that xint recommends updating to NGINX 1.31.9, which was just released, and to block the SCTP module on hosts that do not need it until a kernel fix is available. See the mitigations section of their report for more information.

Note: you can avoid this step in the future by logging into your LWN account.

📅 20 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (860 w)

Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • Recent findings suggest that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

Recent findings suggest that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

In a recent development, the catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Sources indicate that until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

Sources indicate that the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

In a recent development, transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

In a recent development, models too massive for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

Sources indicate that the Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

Recent findings suggest that TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

Industry observers note that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

Recent findings suggest that we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

Industry observers note that the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It has been revealed that it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

Sources indicate that TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch customers. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

It has been revealed that we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.
