Tech Report: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1302 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • It has been revealed that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

It has been revealed that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

Recent findings suggest that the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Upcoming Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

According to recent reports, after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Recent findings suggest that call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

It has been revealed that after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

It has been revealed that the table reveals which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

In a recent development, each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

According to recent reports, in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

It has been revealed that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Industry observers note that replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

According to recent reports, in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

According to recent reports, the table reveals one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Industry observers note that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

According to recent reports, key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that companies are giving AI a bigger role in decisions, but that does not mean their leaders find decisions easier. In a survey published by Körber, 76% of senior decision-makers said decision-making had become more complex. The same share reported allowing AI to play a greater role. The answers describe two trends happening at the same time; they do not establish that one caused the other.

The survey included 2,000 senior executives, split evenly between the United States and Germany. Körber says respondents worked for organizations with annual revenue above $250 million and at least 250 employees, and fieldwork ran from August 27 to September 8, 2026. That makes the findings a look at decision-making inside larger organizations in two markets, not a representative measure of every employer or of small businesses.

The accompanying release says 74% of respondents reported that information volume can get in the way of decisions, while 75% remarked decisions stall when critical information is not available at the right time. Having more data and having the right data when a decision is due are different problems.

Industry observers note that consider a manager who needs to decide whether to delay a shipment. Sales, warehouse operations and finance may have different records for the same order, all updated at different times. An AI assistant can summarize those records quickly, but a faster summary does not establish which number is current or who can approve an exception. Unless the team can check the sources and resolve conflicting records, the tool can move the work of reconciliation from one person to another rather than eliminate it.

The survey also found that 73% of respondents were uncomfortable letting technology make the final decision. That helps explain why businesses may want AI in the workflow without giving it control of the outcome. Drafting an explanation, gathering supporting documents and making a decision that commits the company are separate jobs. The cost of an error differs for each.

Among respondents whose organizations described their transformation as enterprise-wide, 63.8% reported strong organizational performance, compared with 41.6% of those at the pilot stage. Future-readiness confidence was 66.4% and 46.5%, respectively. Intends to invest significantly in AI decision support were almost identical: 59% for the enterprise-wide group, versus 59.4% for the pilot group.

Sources indicate that those are self-reported group differences, not measured returns from a controlled rollout. Organizations that can implement technology across departments may already have stronger data, more resources or better operating processes. The publication does not establish that expanding a pilot causes performance to improve. It is better read as a prompt to ask what mature implementations do differently and which of those practices a particular team can test.

In a recent development, the practical question for an operator is where a tool improves the work between a question and a decision. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework offers a way to formalize responsibilities and decide what to measure in context. Teams can pick a recurring decision and compare how long it takes to obtain the necessary evidence, how often a recommendation must be corrected and whether an approver can explain what they relied on.

Sources indicate that tracking these measures separately can reveal a trade-off that a single adoption number misses. A tool may produce reports faster while increasing the time spent checking them, or it may let people spend less time gathering facts and more time evaluating options. For the executives surveyed, the challenge is not simply making AI more available. It is defining the role it plays when information is incomplete and someone still has to own the decision.

📖 Baca

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In a recent development, in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In a recent development, in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

Recent findings suggest that one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

Industry observers note that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

Recent findings suggest that the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

Industry observers note that the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Industry observers note that think of a shipping organization that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

Sources indicate that and the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Recent findings suggest that adapting a model's vocabulary is not a latest idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

Sources indicate that they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

Sources indicate that they work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

Sources indicate that first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Sources indicate that second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Industry observers note that third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

Sources indicate that an expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

Sources indicate that A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

It has been revealed that the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

It has been revealed that getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

It has been revealed that vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Sources indicate that specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

Breaking: Databricks Brings PostgreSQL 19 to Lakebase and Neon

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, databricks has added PostgreSQL 19 to Lakebase and Neon, giving teams a way to try the open-source database’s newly introduced maintenance, query planning and replication tools on managed infrastructure.
  • The update is relevant to teams building AI applications, even though it does not introduce a latest AI model or vector index.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the main additions in the PostgreSQL 19 release is REPACK, a command that rebuilds a table to reclaim unused space and can optionally reorder the data to match an index.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, databricks has added PostgreSQL 19 to Lakebase and Neon, giving teams a way to try the open-source database’s newly introduced maintenance, query planning and replication tools on managed infrastructure. Databricks claims both services had support on the day the PostgreSQL project released the new version. PostgreSQL’s own announcement dates the community release to November 19, 2026.

The update is relevant to teams building AI applications, even though it does not introduce a latest AI model or vector index. Operational databases often sit behind the user-facing parts of these systems. They store conversation history, track jobs and permissions, record application events and serve calls that need predictable response times. A database upgrade that makes this infrastructure easier to maintain can matter more to those teams than a new feature in the application layer.

Recent findings suggest that one of the main additions in the PostgreSQL 19 release is REPACK, a command that rebuilds a table to reclaim unused space and can optionally reorder the data to match an index. PostgreSQL creates a new row version when data changes. Routine vacuuming makes old space available for reuse, but that does not always shrink the underlying table on disk. A table that stores frequently updated jobs or messages can keep occupying more space than its remaining live rows need.

An option lets ordinary reads and writes continue through most of the rebuild. That does not make the operation free of disruption. As Neon’s release notes explain, PostgreSQL still needs an exclusive lock to finish swapping the rebuilt files into place. Teams should test the operation under a representative write load rather than assume the final lock is negligible on a busy table.

The release also adds pg_plan_advice, an extension for testing and stabilizing execution prepares, and a companion pg_stash_advice extension that can apply stored advice to a matching query. The planner ordinarily chooses how to execute a query based on the data and statistics available. When that choice changes, an operation that used to be fast can suddenly become slow. The fresh tools give operators a way to investigate or mitigate that regression without immediately rewriting application code. Any saved advice should be revisited as the data and workload evolve.

Recent findings suggest that postgreSQL 19 also adds WAIT FOR LSN, which lets an application wait for a database replica to reach a specified position in the write-ahead log. With asynchronous replication, a write can succeed on the primary database before a replica has applied it. A user or agent that immediately reads from that replica may otherwise see an earlier state.

In a recent development, that lag matters if, for example, an application records approval for a task and immediately asks another service to read it from a replica. Waiting for the relevant log position can let that read see the approval. It trades some waiting time for freshness when the workflow needs it, rather than assuming all replica reads are current.

Industry observers note that databricks’ supported-versions documentation lists PostgreSQL 19 for Lakebase, and Neon’s announcement explains how to choose it for a fresh project. Neither announcement indicates that all existing databases were automatically upgraded. Databricks also says Lakebase engineers contributed to the upstream release, including work on query-plan advice, shared memory and release management.

In a recent development, for teams considering a migration, version availability is a starting point. A useful test is to run representative queries, confirm extension compatibility, measure replica lag and rehearse the maintenance operations that prompted the upgrade. Teams can then compare those results with the behavior of their current database before switching production traffic.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF to Secure AI Agents at Scale.
  • Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.
  • Google has confirmed it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two important components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF to Secure AI Agents at Scale.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

Google has confirmed it is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), placing two important components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance. The move is intended to address two emerging challenges in running autonomous agents at scale: securely executing untrusted, AI-generated code and managing the substantial compute overhead created by agents that frequently pause and resume.

According to recent reports, the announcement also includes OpenRL, Google's open-source reinforcement learning orchestration project. Together, the projects target different layers of agent infrastructure, from isolated code execution to managing agent lifecycles and coordinating large-scale training workloads. The goal is to establish an open foundation for agentic applications, much as Kubernetes helped standardise container orchestration.

Google argues that conventional Kubernetes workloads and AI agents have fundamentally different execution patterns.

A traditional application typically starts, serves requests, and continues running. An AI agent, however, may execute a tool or code for a few seconds before waiting for model inference, an external API, or human approval. Google estimates that agents can spend 90-95% of their time idle while still holding crucial state, including memory, files, repositories, and active sessions.

Recent findings suggest that keeping every agent in a dedicated Pod wastes resources, while scaling to zero introduces delays when environments must be reconstructed. At the other extreme, large-scale agent evaluations can overwhelm Kubernetes control planes when thousands of short-lived execution environments are repeatedly created and destroyed.

Google developed Agent Substrate to address these limitations by separating agent state (actors) from the compute resources (workers) used to execute it.

Actors represent individual agent sessions and retain their state, including filesystem contents, memory, and execution context. Workers provide reusable, pre-warmed execution environments drawn from shared Kubernetes pools.

In a recent development, when an agent needs to resume, Substrate assigns it to an available Worker and restores its previous state. When the agent becomes idle, its state can be saved and the underlying compute resource released.

According to Google, this approach lets agents resume in under 500 milliseconds without creating a new Kubernetes Pod for every execution. It also reduces pressure on the Kubernetes control plane by managing agent lifecycles independently of individual Pod objects.

The second major challenge is security. AI agents routinely execute generated shell commands, install packages, and interact with external tools. Treating this code as trusted creates significant risks, particularly when multiple agents share infrastructure.

Sources indicate that google's gVisor provides an additional isolation boundary through a user-space application kernel. Instead of letting containerised applications interact directly with the host Linux kernel, gVisor intercepts system calls and handles them within its own isolated environment.

This reduces the exposure of the underlying host while retaining much of the efficiency associated with container-based execution.

In a recent development, agent Substrate also supports Cloud Hypervisor microVMs for workloads requiring hardware-level virtualisation. This gives platform teams flexibility to select an appropriate isolation boundary without changing the overall agent lifecycle model.

According to recent reports, the announcement reflects a broader shift in cloud-native infrastructure. Kubernetes was designed around long-running applications and relatively stable workloads. Agentic systems introduce more dynamic execution patterns, where environments must be created, suspended, restored, and isolated at much greater frequency.

According to recent reports, other providers are addressing similar challenges through technologies such as Kata Containers, Firecracker, and dedicated sandboxing platforms. Google's contribution is to combine secure execution with an agent-aware orchestration model and place the resulting technologies within an open ecosystem.

The wider implication is that AI agents need more than an orchestration framework and access to tools; they need their own secure, stateful, and efficiently managed execution infrastructure. By donating these projects to the CNCF, Google is helping establish the foundations for that next layer of cloud-native computing.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • According to recent reports, figure 1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Noted It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

In a recent development, we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

According to recent reports, figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

According to recent reports, so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

According to recent reports, we call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

Recent findings suggest that what does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Sources indicate that figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly newly introduced solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

According to recent reports, in our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

Industry observers note that the executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

Recent findings suggest that after training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Recent findings suggest that table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

Recent findings suggest that the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

Recent findings suggest that the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

Recent findings suggest that these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

According to recent reports, figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

It has been revealed that every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

It has been revealed that for the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each enhancement generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Recent findings suggest that zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

Recent findings suggest that no ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Industry observers note that why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

Industry observers note that so we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

In a recent development, figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO revision.

In a recent development, figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

According to recent reports, when sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

According to recent reports, in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

  • It has been revealed that the BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold.

The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.

Recent findings suggest that boodleBox states Montana has approved it as a vendor in the state’s Master AI Products and Services procurement program. The selection gives eligible agencies, colleges and universities a route to purchase the collaborative AI workspace. It does not mean those institutions have placed orders, deployed the product or agreed to use it across the state.

Recent findings suggest that the announcement is an example of a shift from individual employees experimenting with AI to institutions deciding what they can buy and how staff can use it. A department trying a chatbot may be able to start quickly. A public agency or university choosing an institutional service has more to decide: what data may enter the system, which staff can use it, what needs human review and who can see shared work.

Sources indicate that montana’s September information technology board report states its statewide AI solicitation closed with 50 vendors approved. The state estimates that buying from the resulting list can avoid roughly six months of procurement time per solicitation. That is the state’s estimate for the framework, not a measurement of savings from BoodleBox or a promise that any particular order will go through in six months less.

Recent findings suggest that boodleBox’s announcement identifies the tech giant as one of the approved vendors. It did not disclose a purchase value, the number of seats or a deployment schedule. Those distinctions matter because being eligible to sell gives the company access to a purchasing channel, but does not establish actual demand for its software. Montana’s procurement office describes eMACS as the state’s system for managing vendor registration, bids and contracts.

BoodleBox’s product documentation describes a shared workspace in which users can choose from different providers’ models or let the software select one. People can also bring several models into the same conversation. A team could, for example, ask one model to summarize a nonconfidential document and ask another to identify omissions. Those responses are starting points for human review, not independent verification of the document.

Coach Mode adds advice about how to frame a prompt or evaluate a response. Memory Mode can bring information from earlier chats into an answer, while a human-only messaging option lets participants discuss a problem without sending each message to a model. These controls address different needs: a training group might want suggestions to follow an answer, while a team deliberating over an internal decision may want an ordinary conversation. Default settings and sharing permissions determine whether those distinctions are easy for staff to maintain.

Sources indicate that boodleBox says its security and privacy practices distinguish between organization-controlled models and those run by outside providers. In the latter case, prompts and relevant excerpts of attached material may be sent to an outside API, subject to the company’s stated data-handling rules. An institution still needs to assess what can be submitted to each model, how records are retained and whether its agreements address the kinds of information staff handle.

Recent findings suggest that A practical pilot would begin with low-risk tasks and measure both usage and the quality of the result. A university might track how much time staff save drafting course materials, while an agency might count how often a model summary needs substantive correction. The vendor list makes purchasing more straightforward. Whether the software is useful and safe for a specific workflow remains a decision for the institution using it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package).
  • Sources indicate that the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

Sources indicate that the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

In a recent development, at the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We proposal to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script debuts its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

Recent findings suggest that A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel initiative use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

Recent findings suggest that at the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS notes nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space reveals comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

It has been revealed that each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

#92818. How I Got Postgres into a Single Binary

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Progrium ↗ Open Full Page

How I Got Postgres into a Single Binary

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Progrium

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SQLite is one of my favorite database technologies.
  • At the other end of the spectrum is Postgres.
  • According to recent reports, SQLite is a natural fit for software that needs a database but isn't meant to be deployed in the cloud at scale: desktop apps, self-hosted tools, things you run locally.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SQLite is one of my favorite database technologies. It's a full SQL database, designed as an embeddable library, that stores all its data in a single file. The sqlite3 command line tool is great too. You point it at a file and run queries. There's no server to run.

At the other end of the spectrum is Postgres. It's the most capable general purpose SQL database, trusted in production at scale, and is something of an industry standard. With that comes complexity, starting with the fact that it's client-server.

According to recent reports, SQLite is a natural fit for software that needs a database but isn't meant to be deployed in the cloud at scale: desktop apps, self-hosted tools, things you run locally. These applications can use SQLite and manage it themselves, so you barely know there's a database involved.

Recent findings suggest that so when you find self-hostable open source software you'd like to run on your own computer, it can be daunting when it says it requires Postgres. Now you're responsible for setting up a database and getting it ready for the software to use.

According to recent reports, sure, you can run Postgres in Docker, and plenty of projects recommend it. But now you have two dependencies. If you don't already have Docker, you have to install it, which can mean a VM and a daemon on your machine. Then you have to run Postgres in it and make sure it's running whenever you use the software. That's a lot just to try something you don't know you want yet.

Wouldn't it be great to have the SQLite experience, but with Postgres?

According to recent reports, that's miniPG . It isn't Postgres as a library. There's already a WASM project for that, reasonably called PGlite. miniPG is closer to the SQLite CLI: a single program that embeds a full Postgres server and client, wrapped up so you can use it the way you'd use sqlite3. Point it at a path, that path becomes the database, and you can run queries against it right away. There's no server to set up or keep running.

Jumping into a new Postgres database to try something out or debug it is now easier than using Postgres in a Docker container, and you don't need Docker at all. And miniPG still provides a fully functional Postgres server for software that needs one. In many cases, you can just launch an open source program that looks for its Postgres config in the environment with miniPG.

miniPG comes as a single, self-contained executable. You can just point it at a directory and run a query. There's no server to start, nothing to configure, and the result comes back immediately.

That directory is the database. When nothing is using it, it's just files on disk. You can copy it, back it up, or delete it.

This is actually real Postgres, not a compatibility layer, and this binary compiles to Mac, Windows, and Linux.

When some software expects a Postgres server, miniPG can be one:.

Like I mentioned before, it can even launch programs with environment variables that configure it for this Postgres database:.

In a recent development, when the program is terminated, there's no database daemon to leave around or remember to stop. Only the data itself is kept right there on disk, ready to be used next time.

Instructions for getting it and even an interactive demo are available on the miniPG website .

Software people, from developers to open source power people, and agents too, can use miniPG whenever they'd reach for SQLite but need Postgres.

It has been revealed that this really makes Postgres more viable for scenarios it wasn't before. I'd love to hear the use cases I haven't thought of.

miniPG is the result of several attempts at embedding real Postgres into a standalone, cross platform binary.

Sources indicate that the obvious place to start was PGlite. The name says it all, and in a sense it delivers: it's Postgres compiled to WebAssembly. In Go, you can load the module with the wazero runtime, run Postgres inside your program, and have your app connect to it. That's very close to the SQLite library experience.

Brad Fitzpatrick even made a proof of concept that does this in a way that makes PGlite work as a driver for the standard Go SQL package.

In a recent development, the catch is that PGlite only supports a single connection and a single session. Software written for a real Postgres server often assumes it can have more. A common pattern is to start a transaction, then make another query on a separate connection before committing. With only one connection, that second query waits for a transaction that's waiting on it. The app I was trying to run deadlocked.

Industry observers note that if I needed real Postgres, I could run real Postgres in a virtual machine I could embed. I have a soft spot for using webviews as portable containers, so I ran v86, an x86 emulator for the browser, inside one, and booted a full Postgres server in it.

Industry observers note that the rest was plumbing. The headless webview opens a WebSocket back to the host program. Postgres connections are tunneled through it, and Postgres writes its data to a mount served over the same socket. The benefit of this approach is whatever platform the host program runs on, Postgres is always the same build running in the same VM.

I even built webframe for this, a library and CLI for running a native system webview headlessly.

The result was a proof of concept I called postgres-standalone: one binary, any platform, give it a port and a data directory, and you get a full Postgres server. It worked!

Sources indicate that however, it was also an order of magnitude slower than native. Postgres in a VM in WebAssembly in a browser. Initializing and checking a database took a while. In the best case, on my M3 MacBook, it took 7 seconds before it would accept a connection.

I'd already written a design doc for the SQLite-style CLI: give it a directory, run a query, no server to run. On this stack, though, every SELECT * would sit there for 7 seconds first. That ruins the experience, so I had to shelve it. I had proven that embeddable Postgres was possible, just not pleasant.

Later, for unrelated reasons, I built Hyper9 . Inspired by system API translation, an approach that Wine and Valve's Proton are built on, combined with a unique way to use hypervisors, Hyper9 lets you run Plan 9 executables at near native speed on all platforms.

I'll be posting more about Plan 9 soon, but with a little extra magic, I was able to run the same Postgres at near native speed, in isolation, on all platforms. It's effectively the same approach as the previous attempt, but now without the slowdown.

Startup went from 7 seconds to 800ms. So I dusted off the design doc and built it. PGlite was taken, so postgres-standalone became miniPG.

Industry observers note that miniPG isn't a replacement for real Postgres deployments. If you're running in the cloud, using replicas, or serving many users over many connections, use Postgres the normal way.

miniPG is for local, single-user programs: the places SQLite would fit, but you need Postgres.

That said, go ahead and see how far you can push it!

According to recent reports, I'd really like to see how miniPG holds up in the wild, especially across different platforms and architectures. Please try it and tell me what breaks.

Industry observers note that if this works, it proves a model that goes well beyond Postgres: taking complicated systems and packaging them as a single binary for more specific use cases. That's the part I find most exciting, and it's one of many new possibilities Hyper9 enables.

Once a month I send out a newsletter with a little of everything: latest articles, the best of the logs, useful resources, and a few surprises.
